text: Well, the thing is, a valve doesn't die all at once. It gets tired. You'll hear it first, a sort of thinness in the low notes, before any meter tells you. So I don't rush to the tester. I sit with the set for an evening, kettle on, and listen properly. Mind you, half the time it's a dry capacitor and not the valve at all. Anyway. Patience is cheaper than parts.

I'm a poor beekeeper, I'll say that straight off. The bees keep me, more or less. I go out, I lift the lid, I look daft in the veil, and they get on with it regardless. I reckon that's the right arrangement. Anything I've tried to improve on them, they've quietly undone by the next week. Fair enough. They were here first.

The ferry runs twice a day when the weather lets it, and the weather doesn't read the timetable. So you don't plan the day off the timetable, you plan it off the sky. I'll tell you what, the folk who get caught are always the ones who booked something on the mainland at four o'clock sharp. Well. Four o'clock sharp is a mainland idea.

First minute's the argument, and after that the sea's won and you can get on with it. I go in every morning, winter and all. People ask if it's good for me. I suppose it is, as far as I can tell. But I don't go in for that. I go in because the day's not started properly until I have, and that's the whole of it.

Everything in the shed has a place, and if it isn't in its place, it's on the bench being fixed or it's gone. That's the only system. Tomas laughed at it. Mind you, he could find his spanners and I never could find mine, so there's a lesson there somewhere, and I've had nine years to learn it. Anyway. The place is tidy now.

Give me fog over sun any day. Sun's grand for visitors. Fog gives the light a job. You'd stand up there and hear the horn go and know that somewhere out past the skerries somebody was very glad of it. You don't get that feeling from a sunny afternoon. Well, you get a different feeling. A lesser one, I reckon.

topic: letter to the council about the harbour light
text: Dear Council, kindly note that the harbour light has again been out for three nights this month. In short, the bulb you specify is a special order from the mainland with a six-week wait, while a standard marine bulb, which I can source myself for less, would serve. As I said in my letter of last spring, I am willing to fit it. For what it's worth, the fishermen agree.

topic: note left with a restored radio
text: This set is a 1951 Bush, rebuilt properly: new capacitors, the transformer rewound by hand, the original valves tested and kept. Warm it for two minutes before you expect much of it. It will not need a subscription, an account, or a password, and if it fails in my lifetime bring it back to the shed and I will look at it. Keep it out of the damp.

Liv, the swell has been up all week so the Thursday boat did not run and Agnes and I did the crossword by telephone, which is not the same. The bees have settled. I finished the Philips at last; it crackled into life on Tuesday and I sat with it until the shipping forecast. First ferry on the first, as ever. Bring nothing. Mother.

Dear Halvard, your knight to f5 is a nuisance and I suspect you know it. I have taken a fortnight over my reply, which I reckon is within the spirit of our rules if not the letter. Bishop takes. The weather here has been fog for nine days, which suits me and the light both. I trust your knees are no worse than mine.
